results.proposed_proof:
**Given:** The partitions and length bound in the Statement; for part (ii), $|\lambda_i-\mu_i|\le s$, the vectors $\rho,\omega,\delta,D$ and the map $\varphi$ above; $g_0:=n-|\rho|$.

[F1] The internal product is bilinear, $h_m=s_{(m)}$ is its degree-$m$ unit, $s_\lambda*s_\mu=\sum_\xi g(\lambda,\mu,\xi)s_\xi$, and $g$ is symmetric in its arguments ([[def-internal-product-on-symmetric-functions]], [[prop-power-sums-diagonalize-the-internal-product]], [[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]], [[cor-kronecker-coefficients-are-nonnegative-integers-and-s3-symmetric]]).

[F2] Littlewood's identity is $s_\lambda*(s_\tau s_\theta)=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}c^\lambda_{\alpha\beta}(s_\alpha*s_\tau)(s_\beta*s_\theta)$, with $|\alpha|=|\tau|$ and $|\beta|=|\theta|$ ([[lem-littlewood-internal-product-outer-compatibility]]).

[F3] The Schur-product coefficient $c^\lambda_{\alpha\beta}$ counts semistandard tableaux of shape $\lambda/\alpha$ and content $\beta$ with lattice reading word, read right to left in each row and top to bottom. It vanishes unless $\alpha\subseteq\lambda$ and $|\lambda|=|\alpha|+|\beta|$ ([[thm-littlewood-richardson-schur-product-expansion]], [[def-littlewood-richardson-tableau-and-coefficient]]).

[F4] Jacobi–Trudi gives $s_\xi=\det(h_{\xi_i-i+j})_{1\le i,j\le\ell}$ for a partition $\xi$ of length at most $\ell$, with $h_0=1$ and $h_a=0$ for $a<0$. The Schur functions form an integral basis in each homogeneous degree of the stable graded ring ([[thm-jacobi-trudi-and-dual-jacobi-trudi-identities]], [[thm-schur-functions-form-an-orthonormal-integral-basis]], [[def-stable-graded-ring-of-symmetric-functions]]).

[F5] Intersection and union are componentwise minimum and maximum and are partitions; in case (ii), $0\le\omega_i-\rho_i\le s$ and $g_0=\sum_i(\lambda_i-\rho_i)$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).



**Proof technique:** preserve the small skew tableaux by an explicit row shear and apply the first-row Jacobi–Trudi expansion.

1.1 For $0\le q\le n$ and $\eta\vdash q$, apply [F2] to $h_{n-q}s_\eta$ and use the unit in [F1], then extract $[s_\mu]$ using [F3]. This gives the finite coefficient identity $K_n(q,\eta):=[s_\mu](s_\lambda*(h_{n-q}s_\eta))=\sum_{\alpha\vdash n-q,\ \beta,\gamma\vdash q}c^\lambda_{\alpha\beta}c^\mu_{\alpha\gamma}g(\beta,\eta,\gamma)$. Every nonzero summand has $\alpha\subseteq\rho$; writing $e_i:=\rho_i-\alpha_i$ gives $\sum_i e_i=q-g_0$, so $0\le e_i\le q-g_0\le q$. [F1, F2, F3, F5, algebra]

1.2 Assume case (ii), and put $D_{\ell+1}=0$, $\rho_{\ell+1}=0$. One has $\delta_i\le\rho_i-\rho_{i+1}$. If $D_j>0$, let $b\ge j$ be the last index with $\delta_b>0$; telescoping gives $D_j\le\rho_j-\rho_b+\delta_b\le\rho_j-2s$. Hence $\varphi(\theta)_j\ge s$ when $D_j>0$, and when $D_j=0$ its value is $\theta_j\ge0$. If $\delta_j=0$, consecutive parts of $\varphi(\theta)$ have the same difference as those of $\theta$. If $\delta_j>0$ and $j<\ell$, then $\varphi(\theta)_j-\varphi(\omega)_{j+1}=\theta_j-\omega_{j+1}-\delta_j=\theta_j-\rho_j+2s\ge s\ge0$. Since $\theta\subseteq\omega$, this proves weak decrease at every remaining boundary. Thus $\varphi$ maps the stated domain to partitions, is injective, and satisfies $|\varphi(\theta)|=|\theta|-\sum_jD_j$. [F5, algebra]

2.1 Expand the Jacobi–Trudi determinant for $\nu=(n-s,\nu_2,\ldots)$ along the first row. Its $j$th cofactor $B_j$, indexed by $0\le j\le\ell-1$, depends only on $(\nu_2,\ldots,\nu_\ell)$ and is homogeneous of degree $s-j$, since every product in that minor has that degree. Thus $s_\nu=\sum_{j=0}^{\ell-1}(-1)^j h_{n-s+j}B_j$, with $B_j=0$ when $j>s$; for $j\le s$, expand $B_j$ in the Schur basis of degree $q=s-j$. By symmetry [F1], $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)=[s_\mu](s_\lambda*s_\nu)$ is therefore a signed sum of $K_n(q,\eta)$ with $0\le q\le s$. If $|\lambda_i-\mu_i|>s$ for some $i$, then $g_0\ge|\lambda_i-\mu_i|>s$: the sums of the positive row differences in either direction agree because $|\lambda|=|\mu|$. Step 1.1 then has no contributing $\alpha$ for any $q\le s$. Every term vanishes, proving part (i). [F1, F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Put $r:=|\varphi(\lambda)|=|\varphi(\mu)|$. If any $\delta_i>0$, step 1.2 gives $\rho_1-D_1\ge2s$ and therefore $r\ge2s$, so $r-s\ge s\ge\nu_2$. If every $\delta_i=0$, then $r=n$ and $r-s=\nu_1\ge\nu_2$. Thus $\varphi(\nu)$ is a partition. To bound $r$, use $\delta_i\ge\rho_i-\omega_{i+1}-2s$ and telescope to obtain $\lambda_j-D_j\le2s(\ell-j+1)+\sum_{i=j}^{\ell}(\lambda_i-\rho_i)+\sum_{i=j+1}^{\ell}(\omega_i-\lambda_i)\le3s(\ell-j+1)$; the last two sums together equal $(\lambda_j-\rho_j)+\sum_{i=j+1}^{\ell}(\omega_i-\rho_i)\le s(\ell-j+1)$. Therefore $r\le3s\ell(\ell+1)/2\le2s\ell^2$ for $\ell\ge3$. If $\ell=2$, equal total sizes imply $\omega_2=\rho_2+a$ and $n=\rho_1+\rho_2+a$, where $a=|\lambda_1-\mu_1|=|\lambda_2-\mu_2|\le s$; then $r=n-\delta_1-2\delta_2\le(\rho_1+\rho_2+a)-(\rho_1-\rho_2-a-2s)-2(\rho_2-2s)=6s+2a\le8s$. If $\ell=1$, then $s=0$, $\lambda=\mu=\nu=(n)$ and $\delta_1=n$, giving $r=0$. [F5, step 1.2, algebra]

2.3 Fix $q\le s$. The map $\alpha\mapsto\varphi(\alpha)$ is a bijection from partitions $\alpha\subseteq\rho$ of size $n-q$ to partitions $\theta\subseteq\varphi(\rho)$ of size $r-q$. If either set is nonempty, its total deficit from $\rho$ or $\varphi(\rho)$ is $q-g_0\le s$. For the forward direction this proves $\alpha_j\ge\rho_j-s$, so step 1.2 applies. Conversely, given $\theta$ in the second set, set $\alpha_j:=\theta_j+D_j$. These parts are nonnegative and have consecutive differences $(\theta_j-\theta_{j+1})+\delta_j\ge0$. They satisfy $\alpha\subseteq\rho$, $|\alpha|=n-q$, and $\rho_j-\alpha_j=\varphi(\rho)_j-\theta_j\le q-g_0\le s$. This is the inverse. Empty index sets, including $q<g_0$, correspond as well. [step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 For such an $\alpha$, shift every cell $(j,c)$ of $\lambda/\alpha$ to $(j,c-D_j)$. Its image is $\varphi(\lambda)/\varphi(\alpha)$, with each row order and the whole reading word preserved. Within runs of rows with $\delta_j=0$, consecutive rows share columns in exactly the same way. At a cut $\delta_j>0$, the original rows have no common skew column across the cut, since $\alpha_j\ge\rho_j-s>\omega_{j+1}\ge\lambda_{j+1}$. The shifted rows likewise have no common skew column across it, because $\varphi(\alpha)_j-\varphi(\omega)_{j+1}=\alpha_j-\rho_j+2s\ge s\ge0$. The partition inequalities imply the same separation for every row above and below the cut. Thus all column comparisons, weak row inequalities, content and lattice-word conditions are preserved in both directions. Consequently $c^\lambda_{\alpha\beta}=c^{\varphi(\lambda)}_{\varphi(\alpha),\beta}$ for every $\beta\vdash q$, and the identical argument gives $c^\mu_{\alpha\gamma}=c^{\varphi(\mu)}_{\varphi(\alpha),\gamma}$. [F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.3, construct]

4.1 Apply step 1.1 to the reduced outer partitions of size $r$. Because intersection commutes with subtracting the same row vector, their intersection is $\varphi(\rho)$. Steps 2.3 and 3.1 identify the two finite sums term by term, with the same $\beta,\gamma,\eta$ and unchanged $g(\beta,\eta,\gamma)$, so $K_n(q,\eta)=[s_{\varphi(\mu)}](s_{\varphi(\lambda)}*(h_{r-q}s_\eta))$ for every $q\le s$. All degrees are nonnegative: if a reduction occurs then $r\ge2s$ by step 2.2, and otherwise $r=n\ge s$. [step 1.1, step 2.2, step 2.3, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 The first-row Jacobi–Trudi expansion for $\varphi(\nu)=(r-s,\nu_2,\ldots)$ has exactly the cofactors $B_j$ of step 2.1, since its tail is unchanged. Replacing each $K_n(q,\eta)$ by its equal reduced coefficient from step 4.1 in that finite signed expansion gives $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)=g(\varphi(\lambda),\varphi(\mu),\varphi(\nu))$. Step 2.2 gives the asserted size bound, completing part (ii). [F1, F4, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 4.1] ∎

**Given:** The partitions, $k$ and $s$ in the Statement, the shifted partitions $\lambda_t:=\lambda+(t^k)$, $\mu_t:=\mu+(t^k)$ and $\nu_t:=\nu+(tk)$ of size $n_t:=n+tk$; a fixed common length bound $\ell\ge k$ for these partitions.

[F1] The Kronecker coefficient is the tensor-product multiplicity and is symmetric in its three arguments ([[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]], [[cor-kronecker-coefficients-are-nonnegative-integers-and-s3-symmetric]]).

[F2] Steps 1.1–1.2 of [[lem-kronecker-reduction-lemma]] establish, for $0\le q\le s$ and $\eta\vdash q$, $K_n(q,\eta)=\sum_{\alpha\vdash n-q,\ \beta,\gamma\vdash q}c^\lambda_{\alpha\beta}c^\mu_{\alpha\gamma}g(\beta,\eta,\gamma)$, where $K_n(q,\eta):=[s_\mu](s_\lambda*(h_{n-q}s_\eta))$. They express $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ as a finite signed combination of these coefficients whose weights depend only on the tail $(\nu_2,\ldots,\nu_\ell)$. Every nonzero term has $\alpha\subseteq\rho:=\lambda\cap\mu$, with $0\le\rho_i-\alpha_i\le q-g_0\le s$ and $g_0:=n-|\rho|$.

[F3] The coefficient $c^\lambda_{\alpha\beta}$ counts semistandard skew tableaux of shape $\lambda/\alpha$ and content $\beta$ with lattice reading word, and vanishes outside containment and size compatibility ([[def-littlewood-richardson-tableau-and-coefficient]], [[thm-littlewood-richardson-schur-product-expansion]]).

[F4] Intersection and union are rowwise minimum and maximum. Thus $\rho_t:=\lambda_t\cap\mu_t=\rho+(t^k)$, $\omega_t:=\lambda_t\cup\mu_t=\omega+(t^k)$ with $\omega:=\lambda\cup\mu$, and $n_t-|\rho_t|=g_0$ ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).



**Proof technique:** apply the small-skew coefficient identity to the single cut between rows $k$ and $k+1$.

1.1 Assume the row-gap inequality $\rho_k\ge\omega_{k+1}+s$; first-part ordering will not be used. The shifted parameter is $n_t-(\nu_1+tk)=s$, and the shifted tail is unchanged. Fix $q\le s$. The map $\alpha\mapsto\alpha_t:=\alpha+(t^k)$ is a bijection from partitions $\alpha\subseteq\rho$ of size $n-q$ to partitions $\theta\subseteq\rho_t$ of size $n_t-q$. In the forward direction the shift preserves the partition order. Conversely a partition $\theta$ in the second set has total deficit $|\rho_t|-|\theta|=q-g_0\le s$, so $\theta_k\ge\rho_k+t-s\ge\omega_{k+1}+t\ge\theta_{k+1}+t$. Consequently subtracting $t$ in its first $k$ rows produces a partition $\alpha\subseteq\rho$ of size $n-q$, with nonnegative $k$th part since $\theta_k-t\ge\omega_{k+1}\ge0$. All other boundary and row inequalities are preserved. If $q<g_0$, both sets are empty. [F2, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 Shift each cell in the first $k$ rows of $\lambda/\alpha$ horizontally by $t$, leaving lower rows fixed. The image is $\lambda_t/\alpha_t$. There are no shared skew columns across the cut in either shape: originally $\alpha_k\ge\rho_k-s\ge\omega_{k+1}\ge\lambda_{k+1}$, and after shifting $\alpha_{t,k}=\alpha_k+t\ge\lambda_{t,k+1}$. Partition inequalities give the same separation for all rows on either side. Within each side, every horizontal shift is the same, so shared columns and their strict inequalities are preserved. Row order, content and the right-to-left, top-to-bottom reading word are unchanged. This is a bijection of LR tableaux, so $c^\lambda_{\alpha\beta}=c^{\lambda_t}_{\alpha_t,\beta}$ for every $\beta\vdash q$, and the same proof gives $c^\mu_{\alpha\gamma}=c^{\mu_t}_{\alpha_t,\gamma}$ for every $\gamma\vdash q$. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Use the bijection of step 1.1 and the LR equalities of step 2.1 in the finite coefficient sum [F2]. The small partitions $\beta,\gamma,\eta$ and their Kronecker coefficient are unchanged, so $K_n(q,\eta)=K_{n_t}(q,\eta)$ for every $q\le s$. The first-row expansions [F2] for $\nu$ and $\nu_t$ use the same cofactors because they have the same tail. Their signed sums are therefore equal, giving $g(\lambda_t,\mu_t,\nu_t)=g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ for every $t\ge0$. This proves part (i) and also proves that the equality holds under the row-gap inequality without the first-part ordering. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For an arbitrary triple, $\min\{\lambda_{t,k},\mu_{t,k}\}=\min\{\lambda_k,\mu_k\}+t$ and $\max\{\lambda_{t,k+1},\mu_{t,k+1}\}=\max\{\lambda_{k+1},\mu_{k+1}\}$. Thus the row-gap inequality with parameter $s$ holds at $t=t_0$ and for every larger $t$. Apply the ordering-free identity established in step 3.1 to the triple at $t_0$ with further shift $u\ge0$. It gives $G_k(t_0+u)=G_k(t_0)$ for every $u\ge0$, proving part (ii) with the stated threshold for all $k\ge1$. [F4, step 3.1, algebra] ∎
